title: Apollo 13: The Successful Failure
pitchEs: Abril de 1970: tres astronautas van camino a la Luna cuando algo explota a 320.000 km de casa. Una historia real en seis capítulos, uno por unidad.

chapters.title: Live from Space
chapters.body:
It’s Monday evening, April 13, 1970, and three American astronauts are flying to the Moon. Their spacecraft is traveling through the dark at thousands of kilometers per hour, and the Earth is getting smaller in the window every hour.

The crew is finishing a live TV broadcast. Fred Haise is floating in the lunar module, Aquarius, and he is showing the camera how astronauts eat, sleep and move without gravity. Commander Jim Lovell and Jack Swigert are working in the command module, Odyssey. Swigert is smiling, but this week he is living a strange adventure: he is replacing Ken Mattingly, a crew member who was removed from the flight only days before launch because he had no immunity to German measles.

In Houston, Mission Control is following every detail. Flight director Gene Kranz and his White Team are working the evening shift. Engineers are checking numbers on their screens, and somebody is drinking cold coffee. Back home, the world is changing too: for many people, trips to the Moon are becoming routine, and public interest is falling.

Now the broadcast is over. Haise is closing up Aquarius, and Lovell is tidying up in Odyssey. Then the radio comes to life. Capcom Jack Lousma is asking for something ordinary: the crew should stir up the oxygen and hydrogen tanks. Swigert is reaching for the switches.

chapters.title: How a Spaceship Stays Alive
chapters.body:
Before the next two minutes begin, let’s pause the story. How does a spaceship keep three people alive?

Apollo 13 has two spacecraft that fly together. Odyssey, the command module, carries the crew, and for most of the trip it depends on the service module behind it. Inside the service module, two oxygen tanks and two hydrogen tanks feed three fuel cells. The fuel cells combine oxygen and hydrogen, and they produce electricity and drinking water. The same oxygen tanks also give the astronauts the air they breathe.

Aquarius, the lunar module, has a different job. It only lands on the Moon and takes off again, so it carries batteries and a small supply of oxygen and water. It supports two men for about two days. Nobody expects more from it.

On Earth, Mission Control never sleeps. Teams of flight controllers work in shifts, and a flight director leads each team. Usually only one person, the capcom, talks to the astronauts, so the crew doesn’t hear ten voices at once. Every few hours, the controllers ask for routine tasks. One of them is the “cryo stir”: small fans inside the tanks mix the super-cold liquid, so the sensors measure the quantity correctly.

It is a simple procedure, and crews do it many times during a mission. Does anybody worry about it? No. Why would they?

chapters.title: We’ve Had a Problem
chapters.body:
Normally, the crew works quietly at this point of the evening, and the controllers in Houston watch numbers that rarely change. Tonight, things are changing fast.

Swigert turns on the fans. Seconds later, all three men hear a loud bang. Warning lights are flashing. Swigert speaks first: “Okay, Houston, we’ve had a problem here.” Lovell repeats the message a few seconds later.

At first, the astronauts think it is a small electrical problem. But the numbers on the panel are telling a different story. One oxygen tank shows zero. The other one is losing pressure, minute by minute. The fuel cells are dying.

Lovell looks out of the window and sees a cloud of gas around the ship. “We are venting something out into space,” he reports. Oxygen, which gives them power, water and air, is escaping.

In Mission Control, the controllers usually speak calmly and slowly. Now many of them are talking at the same time, and the flight director is trying to keep the room focused. The experts estimate that the fuel cells have less than two hours of life.

The command module is the crew’s home, and it always brings astronauts back to Earth. But this time, Odyssey is slowly losing power, and the mission is no longer a trip to the Moon. It is a fight to get home.

chapters.title: The Lifeboat
chapters.body:
The answer is attached to Odyssey: Aquarius. The lunar module has its own batteries, oxygen and water. But nobody wants to land on the Moon now. The crew wants one thing: to go home.

There is a problem, of course. Aquarius normally needs several hours to wake up, and Odyssey has only about fifteen minutes of power left. Mission Control needs a shortcut, and the engineers find one. Haise knows the lunar module better than anybody, and he moves quickly through the switches. Swigert is being extremely careful as he shuts down Odyssey, because its batteries must survive for the return to Earth.

“What are you thinking about?” a controller might ask his neighbor. Everybody is thinking about the same numbers. Aquarius supports two men for two days. Now it has to keep three men alive for about four days. It seems impossible. Some people in the room think the plan can work; others honestly don’t know.

Inside Aquarius, the astronauts are having a strange night. They hear the hum of the fans. Through the small windows, they see the Moon. It looks enormous, and they don’t feel like explorers anymore. They feel like passengers in a lifeboat, far from any shore.

The Moon is still in front of them, and they can’t simply turn around: the big engine of the service module is too risky to use now.

chapters.teaser: To get home, they must first go all the way around the Moon, and survive the cold, the darkness and an invisible poison in the air.

chapters.title: Around the Moon
chapters.body:
The next days tested everything. On April 14, Apollo 13 swung behind the Moon. For a while, the radio went silent, and the astronauts saw the far side with their own eyes. They traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them. About two hours later, they fired the lunar module’s engine for about five minutes. The burn worked: it made the trip home faster.

Then a new danger appeared. Every breath the men took added carbon dioxide to the air, and the filters in Aquarius couldn’t remove it all. The command module had extra filters, but they were square, and the openings in Aquarius were round. So engineers in Houston found a solution with materials the crew had on board: plastic bags, cardboard and tape. They read the instructions to the astronauts over the radio, and the crew built a strange box they called the “mailbox.” The air became safe again.

To save power, the crew turned off almost everything. In Odyssey, the temperature dropped to about 3 degrees Celsius, and drops of water covered the walls. Nobody slept well. Did they give up? They didn’t. One man always stayed awake and kept watch while the others tried to rest.

chapters.teaser: But one huge question remained: would frozen Odyssey wake up again for the most dangerous part of the trip?

chapters.title: Silence
chapters.body:
On April 17, the crew was flying toward Earth at enormous speed. While Swigert was bringing Odyssey back to life, Lovell and Haise were preparing to say goodbye to their lifeboat. The cold command module worked.

About five hours before reentry, they released the service module. As it was drifting away, the astronauts saw the damage for the first time. Lovell was looking out of the window when he reported the shocking news: one whole side of the module was missing.

About an hour before reentry, they let Aquarius go. The little spacecraft that was never meant to carry them home was floating away into the dark.

Then Odyssey hit the atmosphere. While the capsule was falling through the air, a layer of hot gas surrounded it, and the radio went silent, as it always does during reentry. In Mission Control, many people were waiting in silence. The minutes passed slowly.

Finally, a voice came through the speakers. The parachutes were opening. Minutes later, Odyssey splashed down in the Pacific Ocean, near Samoa, and the USS Iwo Jima picked up the crew. When the astronauts arrived on the ship, people in Mission Control were cheering.

Apollo 13 never landed on the Moon. Lovell later called it a “successful failure.”

chapters.teaser: Odyssey was home. But what caused the explosion? The answer began on the ground, long before launch, and that is another story.
